Seize
sēz
v. (to lay hold of by force; used of a city taken, of death laying hold, and of an inheritance men meant to steal)
Old French seisir, to put in possession. The legal sense — to be seised of an estate — stands behind the parable's use, where the husbandmen intend to possess the vineyard by killing the heir.

Biblical Definition

Joshua uses the word at Ai, and joins it to a promise: “Then ye shall rise up from the ambush, and seize upon the city: for the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand” (Jos 8:7). Men lay hold, and God delivers; the sentence contains both without apology. The psalmist prays it against the wicked: “Let death seize upon them, and let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness is in their dwellings, and among them” (Psa 55:15). But the decisive use is in the Lord's own parable of the vineyard, where the tenants see the owner's son: “This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance” (Mat 21:38). They knew who He was — that is the point of the sentence — and killed Him for the estate. The next verse is the crucifixion in miniature: “And they caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard, and slew him” (Mat 21:39), outside the city, as Hebrews says of Christ suffering without the gate. Seizing an inheritance is the oldest form of rebellion: to have the Father's things without the Father's Son.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines to seize as to fall or rush upon suddenly and lay hold on; to gripe or grasp suddenly; and in law, to take possession of, as of an estate.

expand to see more

SEIZE, v.t. To fall or rush upon suddenly and lay hold on; to gripe or grasp suddenly.

2. To take possession by force, with or without right.

3. To invade suddenly; to take sudden hold of; as, a fever seizes a patient.

Let us seize on his inheritance. Matt. xxi.

Key Scripture

Jos 8:7 — "Then ye shall rise up from the ambush, and seize upon the city: for the LORD your God will deliver it into your hand."

Mat 21:38 — "But when the husbandmen saw the son, they said among themselves, This is the heir; come, let us kill him, and let us seize on his inheritance."

Mat 21:39 — "And they caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard, and slew him."

Psa 55:15 — "Let death seize upon them, and let them go down quick into hell: for wickedness is in their dwellings, and among them."

Modern Corruption

The husbandmen are read as men who mistook the son, when the Lord has them recognise Him first — this is the heir — and kill Him because of it.

expand to see more

A comfortable reading of the parable makes the tenants ignorant: they did not know who He was, and if they had, they would not have done it. The Lord Jesus forecloses that reading in the tenants' own words. This is the heir; come, let us kill him. Recognition is the motive, not the missing element. That matters for how unbelief is understood. Scripture does not present the rejection of Christ as a failure of information which better evidence would have cured; it presents it as a rebellion of the will against a rightful owner, sharpened rather than softened by knowing whose vineyard it is. Romans says the same of the heathen who knew God and glorified Him not as God. The one thing the tenants would not have was a landlord, and the one thing the natural heart will not have is a Lord.

The word carries a further sting in its legal sense. To be seised of an estate is to hold it lawfully; the husbandmen wanted the standing of heirs without the relation of sons, and thought a murder could supply it. That is a fair description of every religion of works, in which a man means to hold the Father's inheritance on the ground of his own tenancy — his labour in the vineyard, his fruit, his long occupancy — rather than by union with the Son. The gospel answers it exactly: the inheritance is not seized, it is received, and it is received only in Christ, joint-heirs with Him. Joshua 8 sets the honest use of the word beside the wicked one. Israel was told to seize a city, and told in the same breath that the LORD would deliver it into their hand; the taking was real, the giving was prior, and no man at Ai supposed the city was his by right of arms.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yarash (H3423), to take possession, to dispossess; nashah (H5378), to lay hold of, at Psalm 55:15; Greek katecho (G2722), to hold fast, and krateo (G2902), to seize.

expand to see more

Hebrew yarash (H3423) — to seize, to possess, to inherit; seize upon the city, for the LORD will deliver it; Joshua 8:7.

Hebrew nashah (H5378) — to lay hold of; let death seize upon them; Psalm 55:15.

Greek katecho (G2722) — to hold down, to possess; let us seize on his inheritance; Matthew 21:38.

Greek krateo (G2902) — to lay hold of by force; they caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard; Matthew 21:39.

Greek kleronomia (G2817) — an inheritance; received by sons in Christ, never seized; Romans 8:17, Ephesians 1:11.

Usage

"“Seize upon the city: for the LORD your God will deliver it” — the taking real, the giving prior."

"“This is the heir… let us seize on his inheritance” — recognition as the motive."

"“They caught him, and cast him out of the vineyard, and slew him” — the cross in a sentence."
